title: Alpha and Omega (Apocalypse 1:8–18)
hook: John on Patmos sees the living one; the letters are cut into the Easter candle

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word apocalypse: not destruction, but an unveiling. Your line was an unveiling. Did something look different once you asked what was behind it? Day six hundred twenty.

It's the dark of Holy Saturday night. Outside a church, a fire is crackling, and a priest holds a tall new candle, the paschal candle, which will stand near the altar all through the Easter season. Following the rite, he may trace a cross into the wax with a stylus. Above the cross, a Greek letter, alpha. Below it, another, omega. Then the four numbers of the current year, one in each corner of the cross. He presses in five grains of incense for the wounds of Christ, and lights it from the fire. The letters he just carved come from the first chapter of the Apocalypse.
screen: `FIRE ON HOLY SATURDAY NIGHT.` → `ALPHA, OMEGA, THIS YEAR.` → `FROM APOCALYPSE ONE.`

segments.voice: Early in the book, God speaks. In the Douay-Rheims: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, saith the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty." Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, omega the last. We'd say A to Z. And A to Z doesn't just mean the two ends. It means every letter in between. Every word that could ever be spelled. Then John tells us where he is: on the island of Patmos, for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. On the Lord's day he hears a voice behind him like a trumpet. He turns around and sees seven golden candlesticks, and among them one like the Son of man. White hair like wool. Eyes like a flame. A voice like many waters. A face shining like the sun. John does what anyone would do. He falls at his feet like a dead man. And then the figure lays his right hand on him. "Fear not. I am the First and the Last." He goes on: I was dead, and now I'm alive forever, and I hold the keys of death. Notice the title. In Isaiah, the first and the last is what God calls himself. Here the risen Christ says it. That's why the priest carves those letters into the Easter candle, saying that all time belongs to Christ, and the ages too. The year we're living in goes on the same wax. Whatever happens between this year's first page and its last, it's inside his A to Z.
screen: `A TO Z, AND EVERYTHING BETWEEN.` · `A VOICE BEHIND HIM ON PATMOS.` · `HE FALLS; A HAND LAID ON HIM.` · `THE YEAR CARVED ON THE CANDLE.` · then, large: `I AM ALPHA AND OMEGA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace A and Omega. With a fingertip, on your palm, a table, or your knee, slowly trace a capital A. Breathe in as you draw it. Then trace an omega, a horseshoe shape with little feet, like an upside-down U. Breathe out as you draw it. Do it again, slowly. Then let the space between your two letters hold your day so far, and whatever's left of it: the beginning, the end, and everything in the middle. If you pray, you can rest in the line, I am the First and the Last. If you don't, just keep tracing and breathing. The bell holds the time.
Patmos, the island. Where John received the vision of the Apocalypse, including Christ's words: I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last. Today's word.
Your line: the first and the last. Today, at the start of something and again at its end, trace the two letters with your thumb. Day six hundred twenty.

howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, the priest marks the new paschal candle with a cross, the letters alpha and omega and the numerals of the year, and may insert five grains of incense; the candle burns at Masses through the Easter season and at baptisms and funerals through the year.

original.note: Greek: the first and last letters of the alphabet (Apocalypse 1:8), carved on the Easter candle.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fancy way to say forever.
what it means: the first and the last letters and everything between: all of time, every day of it, belongs to God.
what a scholar hears: the first and the last is God's title in Isaiah 44:6; the Apocalypse gives it to the risen Christ (1:17).

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the text says the hand was laid 'upon me', not on a shoulder (fixed in teach screen and fork); removed the superlative 'most human moment', 'in many parishes' and the gloss 'a Sunday'; marking the candle now reads as optional ('may').

Easter Vigil: marking the candle with the cross, alpha, omega and the year's numerals, and the five grains of incense, are optional elements in the current Missal. The script describes them as what the priest does; confirm wording (perhaps 'may trace').
The words said while marking the candle are paraphrased ('all time belongs to Christ, and the ages too'); the current English text is not public domain.
Omega described as 'a horseshoe shape with little feet' for the capital Ω. Confirm.
Isaiah 44:6 'the first and the last' as God's title. Confirm.
